newsitem.title: EGYPT: SQUASH-NICOL DEFEATS WORLD CHAMP JANSHER IN CAIRO.
newsitem.headline: SQUASH-NICOL DEFEATS WORLD CHAMP JANSHER IN CAIRO.

text.p: Third-seeded Scot Peter Nicol defeated reigning world champion Jansher Khan in a sensational 92-minute final match of the al-Ahram International Squash Championship in Cairo on Tuesday.

The left-handed Scot beat top seed Jansher 12-15, 15-14, 15- 12, 15-11 in his first tournament win since the 1994 Leeks Classic in Cardiff, Wales. Nicol did however win in an unofficial money match recently played between the two champions in London.
It was second-time unlucky for Jansher who also lost last year's al-Ahram Championship to the fifth-seeded Egyptian champion Ahmed Barada, then a wild card entry.

Nicol said his suprise victory in the glass court, located at the foot of the Pyramids of Giza, was part of a long-range tactical plan. It will also almost certainly elevate his rank to number two in the world.
"I lost the British Open final to Jansher last April but had a good look at him," Nicol said after the win.

"I decided to play him deep in the court to prevent his volleying which he uses to shorten the rally. By keeping him working longer than he likes, I took some of the energy he normally has at the end of matches for a counterattack."

Nicol launched his tactics full-force from the beginning of the match and the Scot soon had the 3,000 spectators who silently watched him beat local hero Barada on Monday cheering him on to a 12-9 lead in the first game of the final.
But the vastly experienced Jansher escaped the deep court net long enough to counterattack stunningly in the front court and clean up that opening game in a single hand.
The patient Scot simply started the second game, went to an 8-5 lead, absorbed another counterattack to 9-9 and then led again 14-12 and game ball.
Jansher might have won that game with a possible penalty stroke after recovering to 14-14 but referee Nasser Zahran allowed him only a let.
Jansher smashed a forehand volley into the tin to lose the single point tie-break. His unforced error swung the match Nicol's way.

Nicol led 6-4, 9-5 and 10-7 in the third game but the Pakistani champion surged again to lead 11-10. But Jansher lost that initiative on a careless penalty stroke in the forehand court and then contributed three more unforced errors to the Scot's call.
Nicol produced a scintillating backhand volley drop under intense physical pressure from Jansher and then followed it with a clinical forehand version to clinch a 2-1 game lead.
Jansher raised the pace noticeably to advance into the front court and built a lead of 10-4.

It seemed he was on his way to a familiar late game surge with which he has killed many opponents but a forehand drifting dropshot that might have continued the resurgence was called down by the referee and had to register as another unforced error.
This gave Nicol the toehold on which to counterattack fiercely and smoothly to close out the game and the championship.

The world champion finished with a desperately low forehand drive into the tin. Nicol finished hands aloft, beating on the sidewalk with the butt of his racket in delight at the reward of his carefully constructed and superbly-played final.

The women's al-Ahram final was, however, an all-Australian affair in which Melbourne's world champion Sarah Fitz-Gerald easily brushed aside her second-seeded Sydney-based compatriot Michelle Martin in just 29 minutes. Fitz-Gerald lead 9-3 9-3 9-0.
